question: Which solvent in the paper has the strongest hydrogen bonding, how strong is it, and why is it not used for delamination?

trace.query: SELECT id, page, text, strength FROM atoms WHERE text ILIKE '%hydrogen%' OR text ILIKE '%δH%' OR text ILIKE '%glycerol%' OR text ILIKE '%water%' ORDER BY page, id
SELECT * FROM cells WHERE table_id='p5.T1' ORDER BY row_no, col_no
SELECT id, page, line_no, text FROM lines WHERE page=6 AND line_no BETWEEN 55 AND 85 ORDER BY line_no

rendered: Water has the strongest hydrogen bonding of the solvents the paper compares. Its hydrogen-bonding strength (δH) is 42.3 MPa^1/2[1], higher than the values for glycerol, diethylene glycol and EG. Water is not used for delamination because it corrodes the aluminum foil: lithium leaching from the NMC cathode makes the water solution basic, and corrosion due to lithium leaching from the NMC cathode[2] ... the resulting aluminum corrosion would contaminate the NMC particles by forming Al(OH)3 precipitates on the cathode surfaces. EG, by contrast, is used because its high δH lets it compete with the PVDF bonding to the aluminum oxide layer without this corrosion problem.
